nodes.question: What gaps in the literature does the paper address regarding Export Credit Agencies (ECAs)?
nodes.answer: The paper addresses the limited systematic analyses of ECA financial flows in the energy sector and the lack of scholarly work on the capacity of ECAs as distinct financial institutions in clean energy finance.
nodes.paragraph: 2021 ; Hughes and Downie 2021 ). Systematic analyses of ECA financial flows in the energy sector remain limited (Censkowsky et al. 2025 ). Similarly, there is a lack of scholarly work on the capacity of ECAs as distinct financial institutions with unique organizational structures, competencies, resources, mandates, and institutional histories to effectively engage in clean energy finance. In this paper, we address these gaps in the literature. We first present descriptive statis - tics of ECA investments from 2005 2023 for select G20 countries. We show that despite some improvements in the post-Paris period, fossil fuel investments remain pervasive and growth in clean energy investments is minimal. For example, ECAs from China and Japan maintained in excess of $4 billion USD in average annual fossil fuel lending since 2015, while Canada and South Korea averaged over $2 billion USD in annual fossil fuel spending. However, there have also been notable increases in clean energy spending amongst some 1340 Climatic Change (2025) 178:40 ECAs, particularly the United Kingdom, which grew its annual clean energy lending from a pre-Paris average of $8.7 million USD to $64 million USD in the post-Paris period.
